# Pattern Transferability and Generalization {#sec-loop-patterns-across-stack}

::: {.epigraph}
> "There is no single development, in either technology or in management technique, that by itself promises even one order-of-magnitude improvement in productivity, in reliability, in simplicity."
>
> — Frederick P. Brooks Jr., *No Silver Bullet* [@Brooks1986NoSilverBullet, p. 10]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *What can be reused across architecture problems, what must be adapted, and what must be re-established?*

**Core thesis:** *Cross-problem transfer requires identifying invariant principles, accounting for distribution shift across workloads and technologies, and recognizing when prior claims must be requalified.*
:::

A new chip program inherits register-transfer level (RTL) modules, simulation scripts, learned surrogate models, and records of earlier trade-offs. Each was qualified under conditions the new program may not share. An array shape tuned for dense matrix tiles can lose its advantage on irregular workloads, while a congestion predictor fitted to one process library can remain confident after its physical assumptions have changed.

Reuse need not mean accepting or rebuilding the whole system. A simulator wrapper may remain useful after the conclusion it once supported no longer answers the new question. The wrapper and the conclusion have different lifetimes, and telling them apart requires tracing which source assumptions still hold on the target. Changed dependencies determine which components need adaptation and which claims need fresh evidence; a changed objective or set of legal designs may require reopening the design question itself.

Two examples run through the chapter. The retained synthetic array experiment shows that a ranking can survive a workload shift while the size of the advantage changes. The prospective Lighthouse application carries useful simulation records into a different power-constrained problem, but the transfer remains unexecuted and establishes neither target power nor implementation feasibility.

## What Transfers Across Chip Designs and What Breaks {#sec-foundations-cross-design-transfer}

Consider a systolic-array tile size selected for one memory system. If the target supplies less off-chip bandwidth per compute lane, the old tile may spend more time stalled even though the array RTL is unchanged. The useful question is which part of the earlier work survives: the tiling principle, the implementation, the search method, or the measured advantage.

Answering that question starts with keeping generalization and transfer apart. *Generalization* describes performance on unseen cases under declared evaluation conditions. *Transfer* tests reuse after a material change from a source problem to a target, while a *distribution shift* changes the population of workloads, designs, or operating conditions represented in the evidence [@QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift]. A method can generalize well to held-out workloads from its source population and still fail on a new target. It exhibits *negative transfer* when carrying its learned relationships or search priors forward produces a worse target result than a comparable target-only method [@WangEtAl2019NegativeTransfer]. These distinctions require a study to state its source and target conditions rather than treating reuse as evidence of success.

Prior work has several forms with different limits. A principle such as amortizing invocation cost remains useful when its assumptions hold. A hardware module or tool wrapper depends on its interfaces and operating conditions. An empirical conclusion, such as one array shape outperforming another, remains attached to the measurements that supported it. Its *support region* is the set of workload, design, tool, and physical conditions covered by that evidence. A changed compiler or library can move the target outside this region even when the direct inputs to a learned model look unchanged.

The operational scope from @sec-three-operational-layers determines what the system is authorized to change in response to a changed dependency. A fixed-template optimizer can retune allowed parameters; a system authorized to revise hardware and software together can also propose changes to the template or interface. Neither scope establishes that the inherited design, method, or conclusion remains useful. That requires tracing the changed dependencies and checking their consequences.

The transfer test in @fig-transfer-test-flow begins by comparing the source and target decisions. A tighter power limit or a new set of legal designs may change the question itself; recalibrating a predictor cannot make the old conclusion answer it. Once the target question is clear, four stages separate reusable work from unsupported claims:

1. **Partition the source into transfer units.** Separate the source record into data, representations, methods, tool interfaces, checks, and configurations. Keep each empirical conclusion linked to the evidence and conditions that supported it.
2. **Isolate the affected slice.** Trace which dependencies and invariants the target workload, interface, or process shift may have changed, distinguishing known violations from relations that still need checking.
3. **Assign target actions.** Designate each unit to be carried forward, updated, retrained, recalibrated, replaced, or retired.
4. **Enforce target checks and test the transfer benefit.** Requalify affected units against target references and compare decision quality and total cost with a matched target-only baseline, including the cost of adaptation and requalification.

![**Transfer testing partitions prior engineering records without porting unverified source conclusions.** An initial admission check evaluates decision compatibility, followed by four stages that isolate affected dependencies, assign unit actions (carry, update, replace, or retire), and enforce target checks on changed interfaces. Unaffected components carry forward while dependent claims are selectively reopened for target validation. The diagram is schematic and carries no measured values.](images/fig-transfer-test-flow){#fig-transfer-test-flow width="80%" fig-alt="Flow diagram of transfer testing, beginning at the source record, whose artifacts, methods, checks, and supported conclusion feed four stage boxes: transfer units separating data, methods, checks, and dependencies; changed dependencies tracing each material change to dependent claims and interfaces; target actions to carry, update, replace, or retire each unit; and target checks on affected units and every interface with a changed neighbor. The flow ends in a target decision box where a new comparison over target measurements supports a new conclusion. A supporting band states that components may move while the source conclusion stays attached to its source conditions and limits."}

Consider a compiler upgrade that changes how a fused attention kernel is tiled onto an accelerator's scratchpad. The accelerator's RTL-equivalence result can remain valid if its compared designs and assumptions are unchanged. The kernel's latency and bandwidth measurements used the old lowering, however, so those claims need new measurements, and the changed command stream needs an integration check. Claims outside those dependencies retain their support. This selective reuse saves work only to the extent that the dependency map captures the change and the checks observe its consequences.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Transfer components, not conclusions"}
**The principle:** When adapting prior design work to new workloads, process nodes, or constraints, artifacts, tool paths, and intermediate data may carry forward, but a source conclusion does not carry forward until the conditions that supported it are shown to hold in the target.

**The application:** Audit the dependency path behind each inherited claim before reusing it on a new target. Require fresh target measurements wherever an underlying workload, interface, or physical assumption has shifted, and retain source support only for claims whose dependencies remain intact.
:::

## Target System Shifts and Decision Reopening {#sec-target-shifts-decision-reopening}

A common transfer mistake is to recalibrate a surrogate or retune parameters when a target shift has invalidated the hardware template itself. Suppose a larger activation footprint causes off-chip transfers that violate the target latency or power bound for every legal tile size in the current memory hierarchy. Recalibrating an on-chip buffer predictor cannot remove that bottleneck; the team must reopen the memory-hierarchy design. The response depends on whether the target changes the conditions of an existing comparison or changes the alternatives and criteria that define the architectural question.

Refining that distinction gives three kinds of target change:

- **Distributional transfer.** The objective, legal actions, artifact boundary, and acceptance criteria remain stable, while workloads, operating conditions, or candidate populations shift. Different batch sizes or a move from dense general matrix multiply (GEMM) kernels to irregular attention can change which array shape uses the available compute and memory bandwidth well.
- **Component or integration transfer.** The core decision remains stable while a component or interface changes along the executable or measurement path. A compiler backend update can alter the schedule; a process-library update can alter timing estimates. Each change reopens the claims that depend on it.
- **New design problem.** The objective, legal actions, artifact boundary, or acceptance criteria change, such as moving from datacenter throughput under a 700\ W-class accelerator envelope to a strict 3\ W mobile or headset thermal limit.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import json as _json9ml
from pathlib import Path as _Path9ml
import _python.plots as _ap9ml

_ml9_dir = _Path9ml(_ap9ml.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data" / "studies" / "12-mlperf-latency-contract"
_ml9 = _json9ml.loads((_ml9_dir / "summary.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
ml9_pairs = _ml9["pairs"]
ml9_logs = _ml9["raw_logs"]
ml9_std_ttft = f"{round(_ml9['latency_contract_ms']['standard_ttft_ms']):,}"
ml9_std_tpot = f"{round(_ml9['latency_contract_ms']['standard_tpot_ms']):,}"
ml9_int_ttft = f"{round(_ml9['latency_contract_ms']['interactive_ttft_ms']):,}"
ml9_int_tpot = f"{round(_ml9['latency_contract_ms']['interactive_tpot_ms']):,}"
ml9_min_pct = f"{100 * _ml9['minimum_interactive_fraction']:.1f}"
ml9_max_pct = f"{100 * _ml9['maximum_interactive_fraction']:.1f}"
ml9_med_pct = f"{100 * _ml9['median_interactive_fraction']:.1f}"
```

These categories apply claim by claim because one target change can affect several dependencies. The size of the change does not dictate the response: a large workload shift may leave the design question intact, whereas a single-line change to an acceptance criterion can alter which candidate is acceptable. Paired server submissions in MLPerf Inference v5.0 show why a stricter service-level objective requires a new comparison (@fig-ch09-mlperf-latency-contract).

![**Submitted server throughput drops under a stricter latency contract on matched eight-accelerator systems.** Paired MLPerf Inference v5.0 closed submissions (`{python} ml9_pairs` system pairs, `{python} ml9_logs` logs) for eight-accelerator Llama 2 70B servers [@MLCommons2025InferenceV50Results]: (a) 99th-percentile latency targets under Standard (`{python} ml9_std_ttft`\ ms first token / `{python} ml9_std_tpot`\ ms per output token) versus Interactive (`{python} ml9_int_ttft`\ ms / `{python} ml9_int_tpot`\ ms) contracts, and (b) submitted Interactive throughput as a share of Standard across H100, H200, and B200 pairs (`{python} ml9_min_pct`% to `{python} ml9_max_pct`%, median `{python} ml9_med_pct`%).](images/fig-ch09-mlperf-latency-contract){#fig-ch09-mlperf-latency-contract width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel horizontal bar chart of 19 matched eight-accelerator Llama 2 70B server pairs in MLPerf Inference v5.0. Panel (a) compares the 99th-percentile latency targets in milliseconds between the Standard contract (2,000 milliseconds first token and 200 milliseconds per output token) and the Interactive contract (450 milliseconds and 40 milliseconds). Panel (b) plots Interactive throughput as a percentage of Standard throughput across 19 NVIDIA H100 SXM, H200 NVL, H200 SXM, and B200 SXM system pairs, ranging from 42.0 percent to 63.9 percent with a median of 58.8 percent."}

In those `{python} ml9_pairs` matched submissions [@MLCommons2025InferenceV50Results], the hardware node and model weights stay fixed while the 99th-percentile latency bound tightens from Standard (`{python} ml9_std_ttft`\ ms time to first token and `{python} ml9_std_tpot`\ ms per output token) to Interactive (`{python} ml9_int_ttft`\ ms and `{python} ml9_int_tpot`\ ms). Sustainable throughput falls to between `{python} ml9_min_pct`% and `{python} ml9_max_pct`% of the Standard rate (median `{python} ml9_med_pct`%). A stricter tail-latency ceiling can restrict batching and scheduling slack, but these submissions do not isolate either mechanism. Their differing throughput ratios show why a comparison qualified under the Standard contract cannot simply be rescaled by a fixed factor when the deployment target shifts to interactive serving.

Whether a change is material therefore depends on the claim and the path that supports it. A library operating-corner change requires new timing and power analysis without necessarily invalidating a compiler-semantics result. Dataset-shift tests can compare reference samples with incoming data to detect departures [@RabanserEtAl2019FailingLoudly], but that signal does not identify the broken physical or software relationship. A detected shift calls for inspecting the affected claims before deciding what to adapt.

The preliminary spatial array experiment introduced in @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization and @sec-feedback-verification-trust makes these distinctions concrete, because its record contains a source result, a shift in its conditions, and a new design question. In that Layer 2 parameter search, SCALE-Sim [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3] evaluated five systolic array shapes on a synthetic three-layer GEMM slice. It swept array aspect ratios within a fixed structural template $\Theta$ and scored them with an uncalibrated cycle-and-utilization proxy. Under that local metric, the source study found a tie and retained the 32 by 32 reference array, a no-change finding that remains confined to its synthetic source context.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Inline values for the transposition probe, read from the retained study record:
#   data/studies/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json
# Score S = total cycles / (average layer utilization as a fraction), lower is better;
# the margin is the loser's score minus the winner's, as a share of the loser's score.
import json as _json9t
from pathlib import Path as _Path9t
import _python.plots as _ap9t

_study9t = _json9t.loads(
    (_Path9t(_ap9t.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data" / "studies" / "ai_systolic_array_study"
     / "recorded" / "reference" / "study_results.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
_probe9t = {e["candidate_id"]: e["metrics"] for e in _study9t["evaluations"] if e["arm"] == "mechanism_probe"}


def _score9t(cid):
    m = _probe9t[cid]
    return m["total_cycles"] / (m["avg_layer_util_pct"] / 100)


def _margin9t(winner, loser):
    return 100 * (_score9t(loser) - _score9t(winner)) / _score9t(loser)


_orig9t = _margin9t("probe_original_16x64", "probe_original_64x16")
_trans9t = _margin9t("probe_transposed_16x64", "probe_transposed_64x16")
_mc9t = _study9t["mechanism_claim"]
assert abs(_orig9t - _mc9t["original_margin_pct"]) < 1e-9
assert abs(_trans9t - _mc9t["transposed_margin_pct"]) < 1e-9
assert _mc9t["observed_original_winner"] == _mc9t["observed_transposed_winner"] == "16x64"
tp_orig_margin = f"{_orig9t:.1f}"
tp_trans_margin = f"{_trans9t:.1f}"
tp_ratio = f"{_orig9t / _trans9t:.1f}"
```

The same record also tests a conclusion under changed conditions. The mechanism probe of @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization ran the $16 \times 64$ and $64 \times 16$ arrays on the original workload and on a transposed version with $M$ and $N$ swapped. On the original workload, the $16 \times 64$ array scored `{python} tp_orig_margin`% better than the $64 \times 16$ array. It still won after transposition, but its lead shrank to `{python} tp_trans_margin`%. The ranking survived the distributional shift; its magnitude did not. A team that carried the source margin forward, for instance to decide whether the wide array was worth its extra modeled write traffic, would have relied on a margin `{python} tp_ratio` times larger than the transposed workload supports. The probe runs a single synthetic three-layer workload under a deterministic simulator and changes several factors at once. It therefore shows that a performance margin need not transfer; it does not estimate how much margins typically shrink.

Selecting an array for implementation in the 3\ W Lighthouse subsystem asks a different question from ranking shapes under that simulator score. The target adds workload, memory-interface, and physical constraints that the source study did not evaluate. Some source artifacts can still help, but the team must separate them from the unsupported implementation conclusion and check each against its target use.

## Untangling a Reusable Block from Its Host System {#sec-decoupling-transfer-units}

Hardware, software, and tools evolve at different rates. A source system therefore needs boundaries at which a team can decide whether a component still performs its intended job. Each *transfer unit* pairs a versioned artifact or method with the relations it assumes and a target check able to test those relations.

### Exposing Dependencies and Choosing Adaptations {#sec-automated-dependency-mapping}

Consider an illustrative cache controller written to consume static random-access memory (SRAM) data two cycles after issuing a read request. Swapping in a denser target macro with a three-cycle read latency silently breaks that controller because the fixed timing assumption was buried in pipeline control logic. A controller that waits for a response-valid indication, such as a ready/valid handshake on the returned data, avoids this fixed-latency dependency; credit-based buffering alone does not establish response readiness.[^fn-flow-control-c09] Such *invariants* are relations that must remain true for a transferred unit to retain its meaning, whether recorded in an interface specification or left implicit in the implementation.

Because such invariants are often left implicit, an automated dependency mapper could help by combining execution logs, source analysis, and environment metadata to flag assumptions a target change might break. Its usefulness could be tested by whether it recovers dependency changes that engineers have checked independently, although recovering known changes would still not prove the map complete. A missed dependency requires correcting the map and widening the affected slice. Reliable mapping across hardware, software, and physical conditions remains an open problem.

In the cache-controller example, a generated SystemVerilog assertion can help expose the latency mismatch if it captures the intended request-response behavior and uses a macro model with the target latency. The assumption and vacuity checks from @sec-feedback-verification-trust still apply: a property that never exercises a delayed response supplies no evidence about that case. A failure blocks reuse under the old timing assumption; a pass establishes only the checked relation, not that every hidden timing dependency has been found.

[^fn-flow-control-c09]: **Credit-based flow control**: A flow-control mechanism where the sender tracks available buffer slots in the receiver using a credit counter, decrementing on transmit and incrementing upon receiving return credit tokens. A ready/valid implementation with an unregistered backpressure path can limit operating frequency across long wires; pipelined buffering can break that path. Credit-based flow control also allows the link to be pipelined across long wires and, when the receiver buffer covers the round-trip latency, to stream without stall bubbles. Credits track buffer space rather than whether a particular read response is ready.

The smallest useful transfer unit therefore has an independently meaningful check. A compiler and its generated binary can be separate units when their identities are fixed and the binary receives an independent behavioral or application binary interface (ABI) check. Otherwise, the lowering path must move and be checked together; splitting it into smaller files would not create independently supported components.

The appropriate adaptation follows from the dependency under test and the outcome of the transfer unit's target check. For a congestion predictor, refreshing target netlists and library metadata corrects stale inputs without changing learned weights. Recalibration adjusts the numerical relation between predictions and observed congestion; retraining changes the learned predictor when that relation cannot be repaired adequately by calibration. If the representation omits a new routing constraint, the team may need to replace it and refit the model. A component that remains inaccurate or costs more to adapt than a suitable alternative can be retired. Held-out target layouts, kept separate from fitting and calibration, test whether any of these actions worked.

The transfer map in @tbl-ch9-transfer-map applies that reasoning to the other parts of a design system. An action is useful only when its accompanying check observes the property affected by the change.

| **Transfer unit** | **Changed dependency** | **Valid action** | **Required target check** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Data and retained knowledge** | Workload coverage, source versions, or collection conditions differ. | Preserve historical records; refresh target samples and sources. | Check provenance, target coverage, exclusions, and source-to-target overlap. |
| **Representation and live state** | A constraint, interface, or represented dependency changes. | Refresh state or adapt a representation that hides a required relationship. | Check version consistency and whether legal target changes and their dependencies can be expressed. |
| **Learned component** | Inputs or the learned relation to the target property change. | Requalify unchanged behavior; recalibrate, retrain, replace, or retire according to the failure. | Test held-out target accuracy, decision errors, and benefit against a target-only alternative. |
| **Conventional method** | An analytical assumption, legal design space, or objective changes. | Adapt the formulation and rerun, or replace it if its assumptions no longer hold. | Compare target results under the same decision rule used for other methods. |
| **Tool interface and environment** | A tool version, parameter meaning, output format, or execution condition changes. | Adapt the wrapper or configuration and rerun affected work. | Exercise target-version execution, parsing, failure handling, and connected-tool behavior. |
| **Checks and decision policies** | Properties, assumptions, reference coverage, error costs, or review capacity change. | Revise affected checks or thresholds; narrow unsupported scope. | Test known valid, failing, and unresolved cases; measure empirical errors against a suitable target reference. |
| **Configured system and conclusions** | Changed neighbors or criteria affect a system claim. | Repeat affected integration and comparison; retain the source conclusion within its original scope. | Measure the target task, including interaction costs and a credible alternative. |
: **Transfer decisions are component-specific.** A unit moves only by assigning an action suited to the broken dependency, paired with a target check observing the resulting architectural risk. {#tbl-ch9-transfer-map tbl-colwidths="[20,28,24,28]"}

The final row matters even when a component's own files are unchanged. A new neighbor can invalidate an integration claim without invalidating the component's local checks. The historical conclusion remains supported under its source conditions; the new system needs its own affected comparisons.

Whether the inherited priors helped at all is a separate question. To test for negative transfer, compare overall decision quality and total engineering cost against a target-only method without source priors. Both arms need the same tasks, budgets, stopping rules, and comparable opportunities to tune on the target. An untuned target-only baseline can make inherited priors appear beneficial merely because the comparison denied the alternative enough adaptation work.

Adaptation costs include tracing dependencies, collecting target data, requalifying carried units, and integrating changed neighbors. A limited pilot can estimate which units are cheaper to adapt than replace before the full comparison. Retiring an unhelpful prior need not discard a qualified simulator wrapper or workload-processing pipeline; both comparison arms can use such infrastructure when the question is whether the prior helps. Reuse can therefore save engineering work even when the target search starts without source preferences.

### Isolating Design Slices {#sec-isolating-design-slices}

Dependency tracking isolates the affected slice so engineers can recheck changed relations and their integration with unchanged neighbors. The boundary must follow the mechanism, not just the source files. Changing a neural processing unit (NPU) from weight-stationary to output-stationary scheduling changes which operands remain local and which move through memory.[^fn-output-stationary-c09] It requires new cycle and memory-energy measurements without necessarily changing the program's mathematical result.

[^fn-output-stationary-c09]: **Output-stationary dataflow**: An accelerator dataflow where partial-sum accumulations remain in processing-element registers until reduction completes. Keeping partial sums local can reduce their memory traffic, while weights and activations still need to reach the processing elements. A weight-stationary schedule instead keeps weights local, producing different buffering and traffic requirements.

Qualifying a unit in isolation is still insufficient when its local choices shift cost onto neighboring blocks. Optimizing a hardware block inside a narrow boundary can push new costs onto global interconnect, off-chip memory traffic, and clock distribution, none of which appear in the block-level report. Machine-learning systems degrade in the same way through hidden feedback loops and boundary couplings [@WangEtAl2019NegativeTransfer; @QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift; @SculleyEtAl2015Hidden].

```{python}
#| echo: false

# Guard for @tbl-integration-overhead: the table cells must match the retained
# SCALE-Sim returns in data/studies/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json.
import json
from pathlib import Path

import _python.plots as _ap

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
_study = json.loads(
    (
        _root / "data" / "studies" / "ai_systolic_array_study" / "recorded"
        / "reference" / "study_results.json"
    ).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
_metrics = {e["candidate_id"]: e["metrics"] for e in _study["evaluations"]}
_base = _metrics["conventional_baseline_32x32"]
_wide = _metrics["ai_wide_16x64"]
assert _base["total_cycles"] == _wide["total_cycles"] == 13917
assert round(_base["avg_layer_util_pct"], 1) == round(_wide["avg_layer_util_pct"], 1) == 41.2
assert (_base["sram_accesses"], _wide["sram_accesses"]) == (491520, 593920)
assert round(100 * (_wide["sram_accesses"] / _base["sram_accesses"] - 1), 1) == 20.8
assert _base["dram_reads"] == _wide["dram_reads"] == 129024
assert (_base["dram_writes"], _wide["dram_writes"]) == (204863, 409726)
assert round(_wide["dram_writes"] / _base["dram_writes"], 1) == 2.0
```

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="Container optimization can hide system cost"}
**The trap.** In a parameter search inside a fixed template, an automated exploration engine optimizes parameters $\theta \in \Theta$ within a fixed structural container against a local proxy metric, and a local win or tie is read as a system-level result.

**The mechanism.** In the retained systolic array study (@tbl-integration-overhead), a wider $16 \times 64$ geometry ties the $32 \times 32$ baseline on the score's cycle count (excluding prefetch) and on the local score, yet SCALE-Sim reports twice as many modeled DRAM-word writes and more SRAM accesses [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3]. The container holds the memory interface and dataflow fixed, and the score never sees that traffic. The run did not model DRAM timing or energy, so the difference exposes a question the local score cannot answer rather than a measured system penalty.

| Returned quantity | $32 \times 32$ baseline | $16 \times 64$ candidate | Difference |
|:---|---:|---:|:---|
| Cycles excluding prefetch | 13,917 | 13,917 | Tied |
| Average layer utilization | 41.2% | 41.2% | Tied |
| Modeled SRAM accesses | 491,520 | 593,920 | $+20.8\%$ |
| Modeled DRAM-word reads | 129,024 | 129,024 | Identical |
| Modeled DRAM-word writes | 204,863 | 409,726 | $2.0\times$ |
: **A tied local score conceals a doubling of modeled write traffic.** Retained SCALE-Sim returns for the two tied candidates in the systolic array study. The scored cycle field excludes prefetch, so the tie does not establish equal end-to-end latency. Traffic counts are idealized word counts (no DRAM timing model) and carry no energy or power estimate [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3]. {#tbl-integration-overhead tbl-colwidths="[34,22,22,22]"}

**The lesson.** Bound such searches and transfer checks to the smallest enclosing boundary that captures interconnect, memory traffic, and thermal coupling, and report what the local score omits. When a quantity outside the container decides the question, the container cannot settle it; the study must widen its measurement, and possibly reopen the interface, before any system claim is made.
:::

Widening the measurement does not dissolve the block as a transfer unit. Its locally checked properties can still carry forward, while any system-level power or latency claim requires an enclosing-boundary check that measures traffic and timing between blocks directly.

### Validating Transfer Conditions {#sec-validating-transfer-conditions}

The target check must exercise the changed relation, not merely confirm that the component still runs. A simulator wrapper can pass its syntax regressions while forwarding out-of-range parameters introduced by a neighboring representation. The target tests need to include those values and verify both the expected rejection and the valid boundary cases.

The qualification rules from @sec-feedback-verification-trust apply to the result. An old proof remains useful only where its property, model, and assumptions still match; a predictor needs target error measurements against a reference that observes the claimed property. Checks that share a model or specification can retain the same blind spot after transfer. Component checks therefore have to be combined with integration tests wherever the claim depends on interactions [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden]; they are not interchangeable votes that the transferred system works.

## Transfer Under Distribution Shift {#sec-transfer-distribution-shift}

A shift becomes actionable when the team can connect a changed condition to a relationship the source method relied on. Different failures call for different adaptations. New workload samples may be enough to retune an existing schedule; changed memory-ordering rules may require new synchronization; a different metal stack may require refitting a predictor against routed target designs. The source artifact's continued execution does not distinguish these cases.

For workload transfer, start with the program and its mapping. A dense matrix workload supplies regular tiles and steady data reuse, whereas mixture-of-experts token routing changes tile sizes and work balance, and autoregressive decoding increases repeated memory traffic. Representative target traces must therefore measure utilization and bandwidth together. A fall in utilization can call for changing the mapping or data-movement schedule before replacing the array hardware. Workload characterization should separate intrinsic program properties from the effects of a particular machine [@HosteEeckhout2007MICA]. Compiler autotuners such as AutoTVM and Ansor show why the distinction matters, because their cost models are fitted to measurements of workloads and candidate schedules on one hardware target [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @ZhengEtAl2020Ansor]. A new workload or mapping can therefore change the conditions supporting both the tuned schedule and the fitted model even when the hardware is unchanged. Both require target checks to determine what remains valid.

An instruction set architecture (ISA) change can break a functional relation rather than a performance prediction. Consider message passing in which a producer writes a payload before setting a flag, and a consumer reads that payload after observing the flag. Under RISC-V Weak Memory Ordering (RVWMO), explicit synchronization must preserve those relationships [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]. For ordinary memory accesses, producer-side `fence w, w` and consumer-side `fence r, r` illustrate the ordering obligations that source-language atomics and compiler lowering must also maintain. The invariant is visibility of the payload after the flag is observed, not preservation of the source instruction sequence. Target litmus tests, small concurrent programs that expose permitted memory-access interleavings, exercise that relation. Passing a single-core test would leave it untested.

A process migration changes the relation between circuit structure and physical behavior. A congestion predictor fitted to one library and metal stack can retain a useful netlist representation while losing the accuracy of its fitted predictions. Moving power routing to the backside of the wafer, for example, changes the frontside resources available for signal routing.[^fn-bspdn-c09] The team should compare predictions with held-out routed target layouts before deciding whether recalibration suffices or the model needs new features and training. CircuitNet supplies measured design data, and ChiPBench evaluates placement algorithms against final power, performance, and area; both show what such implementation references look like [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet; @WangEtAl2025ChiPBench]. A changed node label alone establishes neither successful transfer nor model failure.

[^fn-bspdn-c09]: **Backside power delivery network (BSPDN)**: An arrangement that routes power through the backside of the silicon wafer, separating the power-delivery network from frontside signal routing. Its resistance and routing benefits depend on the implemented network and device connections, and a migration to backside power can invalidate relationships fitted to a frontside-power stack.

A package change similarly requires a new model for the boundaries that traffic crosses. A die-to-die interface such as Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) adds interface circuitry, protocol adaptation, and bump parasitics [@UCIeConsortium2026Spec].[^fn-die-interconnect-latency-c09] The transfer check traces which traffic crosses each boundary, measures its volume and timing, and compares the resulting demand with the target link's bandwidth and energy under declared conditions. Keeping intermediate results on a die or wafer removes some crossings but does not eliminate input and output traffic. A local bandwidth advantage becomes a system advantage only after those remaining costs are included.

[^fn-die-interconnect-latency-c09]: **Die-to-die interface overheads**: Short-reach interfaces still pay for transmit and receive circuits, protocol adaptation, and bump capacitance. Partitioning a tightly coupled systolic array or shared-cache coherence domain across a die boundary without accounting for those costs can make a monolithic performance model optimistic.

These adaptations preserve useful source work while replacing the relations that no longer describe the target. Software updates create the same problem over time. The hardware can remain fixed while a new compiler or runtime changes the executed schedule and the result it supports.

## Version Dependencies and Interface Contracts {#sec-version-dependencies-contracts}

A software update can change whether accelerator offload pays without changing the accelerator. The compact LogCA analysis in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales separates fixed invocation cost from transfer cost that grows with the workload. Compiler fusion can create larger payloads that amortize invocation overhead while eliminating intermediate data transfers. A target compiler that fuses less can therefore move the same hardware onto the wrong side of break-even. A transferred offload result carries its software path with it, including the generated code, runtime, and interfaces that produced the measured traffic and latency.

The hardware-software version pair also determines how a candidate uses the datapath. Changing an array's dimensions without adapting its compiler tiling can produce partial tiles or unaligned transfers; a measured slowdown may reflect that mismatch rather than a limit of the revised array. Pinning both versions makes the result identifiable, but it does not remove the interaction. Comparisons with an earlier baseline need the compatible dependency versions and inputs that produced it, and a hardware claim needs tests that distinguish datapath effects from software effects.

Public MLPerf submissions show why performance gains cannot be carried across version pairs by a fixed factor (@fig-ch09-mlperf-software-dividend). Between MLPerf Training v2.1 (November 2022) and v3.0 (June 2023), NVIDIA's submissions with eight H100-SXM5-80GB GPUs improved by different amounts across three workloads. Ratios calculated from the published times reach $1.166\times$ for BERT, $1.084\times$ for ResNet-50, and $1.082\times$ for 3D U-Net [@MLCommons2022TrainingV21Results; @MLCommons2023TrainingV30Results]. NVIDIA attributes the gains to software updates including fused attention, CUDA graph capture, GEMM library improvements, and convolution kernels [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware]. The GPU model and count match, but the earlier preview record leaves clock, host-memory, and detailed software fields unspecified. The public records therefore neither verify that the complete machine was unchanged nor isolate a compiler effect.

![**H100 training results improve by different amounts across workloads.** Speedups divide published MLPerf Training v2.1 times (preview result 2.1-2091) by v3.0 times (available results 3.0-2064 for BERT and 3.0-2062 for ResNet-50 and 3D U-Net) [@MLCommons2022TrainingV21Results; @MLCommons2023TrainingV30Results]. All rows list eight H100-SXM5-80GB GPUs, so per-accelerator normalization gives the same ratios. NVIDIA attributes the gains to software optimization [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware]; incomplete preview metadata limits independent claims about whole-system identity and causal attribution.](images/fig-ch09-mlperf-software-dividend){#fig-ch09-mlperf-software-dividend width="80%" fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart of published time-to-train ratios for eight H100-SXM5-80GB GPUs from MLPerf Training v2.1 to v3.0: BERT 1.166 times, ResNet-50 v1.5 1.084 times, and 3D U-Net 1.082 times. The earlier submission was a preview system."}

The gains differ across workloads even within this version pair, so the BERT ratio does not describe the observed improvement on ResNet-50 or 3D U-Net. Nor does the comparison establish a gain for later releases. An architect must retain software history alongside hardware specifications and remeasure the target configuration before attributing an improvement to microarchitecture.

The inverse risk appears when a generated hardware candidate uses an immature compiler backend while the production baseline benefits from years of operator fusion. The end-to-end comparison describes the two available systems, which may be the relevant deployment question. Isolating their microarchitectures requires further work, such as tuning both candidates under matched budgets or perturbing tile sizes to test whether a result depends on a favorable compiler schedule. These checks carry the versioned source result into a target comparison without assuming either that every software change invalidates it or that fixed hardware preserves it.

## Cross-Stack Pattern Transfer {#sec-cross-stack-pattern-transfer}

Applying the transfer test to our prospective Lighthouse subsystem begins with a new target question: which array and memory organization can serve the workload within the 3\ W budget? The retained array sweep supplies candidate identities, simulator returns, and a wrapper, but its no-change recommendation applies only to the synthetic GEMM slice. Workload traces, compiler mappings, target energy models, and implementation evidence are still missing. The following application is a study plan, not an executed transfer or permission to freeze the array interface.

Two source units require different actions. A pending rerun under the pinned source configuration would check whether the SCALE-Sim wrapper reproduces the retained cycle and utilization counts; it would not qualify a Lighthouse power prediction. The source decision rule needs replacement because its ratio of cycles to utilization omits memory traffic (@sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration). The simulator did record word traffic, which can inform a new comparison, but those counts alone do not establish power.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Derived, not measured: energy of the extra modeled DRAM writes of the 16 x 64 candidate.
# Inputs:
#   extra writes   data/studies/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json
#   pJ per access  data/datasets/chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv, "DRAM access, 64 bit" (Horowitz, ISSCC 2014, 45 nm)
# Assumption: each modeled word costs one full 64-bit DRAM access.
# The target execution rate is unknown; no other traffic, refresh, or interface energy is counted.
import csv as _csv9e
import json as _json9e
from pathlib import Path as _Path9e
import _python.plots as _ap9e

_root9e = _Path9e(_ap9e.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
_st9e = _json9e.loads((_root9e / "data" / "studies" / "ai_systolic_array_study" / "recorded" / "reference" / "study_results.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
_m9e = {e["candidate_id"]: e["metrics"] for e in _st9e["evaluations"]}
_extra9e = _m9e["ai_wide_16x64"]["dram_writes"] - _m9e["model_baseline_32x32"]["dram_writes"]
with open(_root9e / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter2-horowitz-energy.csv", encoding="utf-8") as _fh:
    _dram9e = next(r for r in _csv9e.DictReader(_fh) if r["operation_or_access"] == "DRAM access")
_pj_lo9e, _pj_hi9e = float(_dram9e["energy_low_pj"]), float(_dram9e["energy_high_pj"])
_mj_lo9e = _extra9e * _pj_lo9e * 1e-9
_mj_hi9e = _extra9e * _pj_hi9e * 1e-9
en_extra_writes = f"{_extra9e:,}"
en_pj_lo = f"{_pj_lo9e / 1000:.1f}"
en_pj_hi = f"{_pj_hi9e / 1000:.1f}"
en_mj_lo = f"{_mj_lo9e:.3f}"
en_mj_hi = f"{_mj_hi9e:.3f}"
```

A derived estimate makes the missing quantities explicit. The $16 \times 64$ candidate issues `{python} en_extra_writes` more modeled DRAM-word writes per pass of the workload slice than the baseline. If each extra word costs one full 64-bit access, its additional write energy and average power are

$$
\Delta E_{\mathrm{writes}} = \Delta N_{\mathrm{writes}} E_{\mathrm{access}},
\qquad
\Delta P_{\mathrm{writes}} = \Delta E_{\mathrm{writes}} f_{\mathrm{slice}},
$$

where $f_{\mathrm{slice}}$ is the number of slice executions per second. Substituting the historical `{python} en_pj_lo` to `{python} en_pj_hi`\ nJ per 64-bit access reported by @Horowitz2014Energy gives `{python} en_mj_lo` to `{python} en_mj_hi`\ mJ per pass under that assumption. The figure is only approximate, because the write count is a simulator return and the energy input comes from an older process node and memory interface rather than from measurement on Lighthouse. Charging a full access per modeled word also overstates energy whenever narrower words are packed into bursts. Even this per-pass estimate cannot establish power because the target execution rate $f_{\mathrm{slice}}$ remains unknown. Testing the 3\ W constraint therefore requires a calibrated energy model, measured execution rates, and the rest of the subsystem power budget. Until those exist, the source score cannot admit any array shape for implementation, including the retained 32 by 32 reference.

An automated transfer harness that carries the source comparator forward could incorrectly describe the reference array as power-qualified. The error would be an unsupported power conclusion, not a demonstrated 3\ W violation. A memory-aware target comparison might retain that array, choose another, or reject every candidate. Leaving all three outcomes open lets the source artifacts help without letting the source verdict decide a different problem.

If no legal configuration within the source template meets the target constraints, the team must reopen the organization rather than keep tuning its dimensions. Conventional redesign or an AI-native design system could propose different memory structures and software schedules. Neither route has been executed for this transfer, and each would need its own target comparison and the checks appropriate to its implementation claims.

The resulting plan assigns a concrete action to each source unit (@tbl-ch9-target-tests). It preserves useful infrastructure while making the missing target evidence visible.

| **Source unit** | **Target action and check** | **Claim left open** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Synthetic workload and candidate set** | Collect representative Lighthouse traces, including tail cases; declare legal target candidates and a credible comparator. | Source coverage and ranking do not establish the preferred target organization. |
| **SCALE-Sim wrapper and fast screen** | Check source replay, then compare the screened target properties with a reference capable of observing them. Measure errors on both promoted and rejected candidates. | Executable reuse does not establish predictive validity or safe rejection of target candidates. |
| **Cycles-to-utilization score and traffic counts** | Replace the score with target latency and power criteria. Bind traffic to calibrated access energy, execution rate, and the rest of the subsystem budget. | No 3\ W or system-speedup claim follows from source counts. |
| **Mapping and memory-interface assumptions** | Generate and execute target software under pinned compiler and runtime versions; measure communication and check the changed interfaces. | A simulator configuration does not establish that target software can use the array correctly or efficiently. |
| **Proposed hardware organization** | Evaluate behavior and physical properties with models, libraries, and implementation flows qualified for the target process and claimed conditions. | No implementation-feasibility claim beyond the completed checks. |
| **Inherited search priors** | Compare with a target-only search under matched tasks, budgets, and stopping rules, charging adaptation and requalification to reuse. | Retaining a prior does not establish transfer benefit. |
: **The Lighthouse transfer plan preserves source artifacts while replacing unsupported target claims.** These actions remain prospective; missing checks leave the corresponding conclusions unresolved. {#tbl-ch9-target-tests tbl-colwidths="[25,45,30]"}

The screen row separates a runnable tool from a useful target filter. Its errors and coverage must be measured against a target reference before the screening economics from @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization apply. Checking only promoted candidates would miss viable alternatives rejected by the inherited screen. If the inherited search prior in the final row harms the comparison, the team can retire it while retaining the wrapper and historical records. For Lighthouse, a supported transfer decision might therefore reuse the SCALE-Sim infrastructure while starting the target search without source preferences.

## Open Questions {#sec-patterns-open-questions}

When we carry models, tools, and design records across workloads, compilers, process nodes, or packages, five open research questions remain:

- **When we reuse a fast screening model on a new target, how do we keep it from quietly ruling out the best candidate designs?** If a team checks a source-trained surrogate only on target candidates it promoted, that test catches weak designs that were wrongly promoted, yet it says nothing about viable architectures that the stale filter rejected before physical evaluation. When a workload shifts from dense matrix tiles to irregular sparse attention or a floorplan moves to a new metal stack, a conservative surrogate can discard the exact structural changes the target problem needs without raising an error flag. A team can spot-check a random subset of rejected candidates with a reference simulator or place-and-route flow to expose those missed opportunities, but every audit spends compute budget that could otherwise evaluate top-ranked proposals. We still lack practical ways to pair shift-aware uncertainty estimates with adaptive spot checks, so that a team can bound how much performance the filter may be missing as the search distribution changes.

- **How can we tell whether a hardware speedup will survive a change in compiler scheduling without running a full autotuner on every candidate?** When a team pins the compiler snapshot, a source-to-target comparison becomes reproducible, yet that freeze also locks in scheduling heuristics that may favor one candidate by accident. An accelerator can outperform its baseline simply because its scratchpad capacity and systolic dimensions divide evenly into a Triton or Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) loop-tiling pass. The measured gain then comes from a fragile match between one datapath and one lowering heuristic, not from a durable hardware improvement. An architect can expose those brittle wins by perturbing problem dimensions or retuning schedules for each candidate, but running a full compiler autotuner inside every hardware evaluation quickly exhausts the search budget. We still need low-cost sensitivity checks and representations that separate a datapath's underlying capability from a lucky compiler alignment before the hardware interface is frozen.

- **How can we separate what a learned timing or congestion model captures about circuit structure from the physics of a single process node?** Graph-based surrogates combine netlist topology with cell delays, metal pitches, and pin-access rules from their training data. A process migration can break those fitted relationships even when the RTL is unchanged. A representation that separates logic connectivity from process-specific physical parameters could reduce the routed target layouts needed for adaptation. The unresolved question is how to preserve useful structural knowledge while re-establishing prediction accuracy near timing and congestion limits.

- **When a team modifies one block on a die, how can it tell which unedited neighbors still have valid timing and power evidence without rerunning full-chip signoff?** Selective requalification saves engineering time only when the dependency map catches every property a target change can disturb. Incremental timing analysis[^fn-incremental-sta-c09] updates arrival times along modified logic cones [@OpenROADDocs]. Repositioning an SRAM macro or resizing a tile buffer, however, can also shift clock-tree insertion delay, capacitive crosstalk, and dynamic voltage drop across neighboring blocks that share no logical wires with the edited module. A dependency check that follows only structural netlist connectivity understates the affected slice, whereas rerunning full-chip extraction and electrothermal signoff after every local edit wipes out the time savings of modular transfer. We still lack fast physical-sensitivity bounds that can be paired with structural dependency graphs to tell an architect when an unedited neighbor's timing and power evidence remains valid.

[^fn-incremental-sta-c09]: **Incremental static timing analysis**: An optimization in physical design signoff where timing graphs are updated only for logic cones and net parasitics directly affected by an incremental circuit or placement modification, rather than recomputing the full chip. In a transfer setting, an incremental update understates the change if macro repositioning alters global clock-tree insertion delay or coupling on neighboring paths that the update treats as undisturbed.

- **How can we predict whether a block-level performance or power advantage will survive when a design is split across chiplets?** Chiplets joined by die-to-die links such as UCIe promise modular hardware reuse, letting teams assemble previously qualified compute dies and memory controllers into new product tiers without full-chip redesign. Even when each die's internal RTL and local timing closure carry forward intact, a design that splits a shared coherence domain or systolic dataflow across dies on a package substrate pays for protocol-adapter latency, bump capacitance, and thermal coupling between stacked or adjacent dies. Single-die performance and power models miss those boundary penalties, while full multi-die cosimulation is too slow for early exploration. We still need interface-level abstractions and contracts that let an architect predict when a block-level advantage will hold up in a multi-die package before committing to substrate routing and thermal verification.

## Summary {#sec-patterns-summary}

Transfer begins by asking whether the target preserves the design question, then tracing which supporting relationships changed. The array probe showed that even a surviving ranking can carry a different margin; the prospective Lighthouse application showed why retained simulator outputs cannot establish a new power or implementation claim. Separating artifacts, methods, and conclusions lets a team preserve useful work while adapting the parts that determine the target result.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Components move, conclusions do not.** Data sources, models, tool paths, and checks remain reusable while their invariants and dependencies hold, whereas a source conclusion applies only where its supporting conditions still hold and requires new evidence whenever dependencies change.
- **Check the decision before the components.** An admission check asks whether the question itself changed; unit actions and target checks follow only once that is settled, and a changed question reopens every claim tied to it.
- **Materiality is claim-specific.** A change reopens a claim when it alters the candidate identity, executable path, measured quantity, objective, decision rule, ranking, constraint verdict, or physical mechanism; magnitude alone decides nothing.
- **Transfer benefit needs a matched arm.** A carried prior earns its place only against a target-only arm with the same tasks, budgets, and stopping rules, with adaptation and requalification charged to the transfer.
- **A transferred result carries its compiler version.** Retain hardware and software snapshots with the inputs and procedures needed to repeat a comparison, and test software sensitivity before attributing a gain to microarchitecture, since a comparison that pins the hardware but not the toolchain can mistake compiler maturity for a hardware gain.
:::

Transfer testing asks whether prior work remains useful under changed conditions, including the integration checks needed for the new target. The broader question is whether the complete AI-native approach improves architectural results or reduces the total effort needed to obtain them. Answering it requires separating the contributions of candidate designs, methods, configured systems, and human work, then testing each comparison against credible alternatives and misleading measures of success (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect).
